 Preview: KU faces difficult test with No. 10 BYU on senior day
 By Henry Greenstein     Nov 20, 2026
 Kansas head coach Lance Leipold watches the video board during a UCF drive late in the fourth quarter on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026 at David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium. Nick Krug/Special to the Journal-World 
 When the Kansas football team stormed back late in the 2024 season as it made a final charge for bowl eligibility, it had to take down BYU along the way.
 That year’s Jayhawks, at 3-6, stunned the unbeaten Cougars 17-13 in Provo, Utah. This year’s team, which is 4-6 after blowing out West Virginia on the road last week, will come up against another top-10-ranked BYU team on Saturday at 11 a.m. at David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium. The game will serve as KU’s senior day and an opportunity to earn one of the Jayhawks’ most memorable wins under head coach Lance Leipold.
 “We have to find a way to just get through them,” KU running back Chase Belcher said. “It’s really the same game plan as every week. We don’t really change anything different. Like Coach says, we don’t plan to win and we don’t plan to lose.”
 BYU sits at No. 10 in the College Football Playoff ranking, in large part because it has one of the most impressive results by any team in the country this season, a 28-24 triumph over then-No. 2 Notre Dame at LaVell Edwards Stadium on Oct. 17. 
 Unlike the unbeaten team that KU took down two years ago, this group of Cougars has already taken its lumps — a 39-31 double-overtime loss at UCF immediately after that game against the Irish, then a loss to Utah in the Holy War — but it remains very much in contention for a Big 12 championship spot and a College Football Playoff berth.
 “They are extremely physical in all areas,” Leipold said. “You look at receivers with great size, length, speed, physical runners, quarterback plays in a physical mindset. Defensively, play aggressively downhill. A lot of depth that they can rotate, stay fresh, come at you. They play with a lot of confidence as well.”
 BYU comes to Lawrence after a ho-hum 28-7 win against Baylor on Saturday. It was the second game back for star running back LJ Martin, the Big 12’s preseason offensive player of the year who had missed a month due to an ankle injury; however, after a Bear defender inadvertently stepped on the ankle, he sat out the second half, apparently as a precaution, and has no injury designation this week.
 Martin is averaging 7.2 yards per carry this season, but he also has just 15 carries for 84 yards since Sept. 19. In his absence, the Cougars deployed several backup running backs, but the primary engine of their offense has been quarterback Bear Bachmeier. The second-year starter has thrown for 2,126 yards with a 62.3% completion percentage, 14 touchdowns and eight interceptions. In part because of Martin’s situation, he is also BYU’s leading rusher with 449 yards and 10 more touchdowns.
 “He’s a winner,” KU defensive coordinator D.K. McDonald said. “We were talking in there as coaches, man, he reminds you a little bit of a Tim Tebow type, just the thick body he has there, he can throw the ball, he can run hard, he’s probably not going to be the guy juking you like we played last week (West Virginia’s Michael Hawkins Jr.), but man, he’ll run through your face.”
 The offensive line protects Bachmeier well — BYU has allowed just six sacks, which ranks fourth in the nation — and the Cougars have recruited well to surround him with weapons. McDonald said they have two NFL-caliber wideouts. Legend Glasker has dazzled as a true freshman with a team-high 42 catches for 706 yards and five touchdowns. Oregon transfer Kyler Kasper, who stands 6-foot-6, has grabbed five scores of his own. And USC transfer tight end Walker Lyons has been one of the league’s best at his position, too.
 With all that talent, though, BYU isn’t necessarily one of the most statistically productive offenses — it ranks in the middle of the Big 12 in scoring and 13th in total yards. 
 The defense has far more impressive numbers, including giving up just 295.8 yards per game, which leads the Big 12 and is 20th nationally. The Cougars are especially stout against the run, allowing just 100.3 yards on the ground.
 “They’re intelligent on defense,” KU associate head coach Andy Kotelnicki said. “They’re well coached. They have a lot of depth. They play a lot of guys different spots and they run around really, really well, so we’ll have our hands full again.”
 BYU has a strong, albeit injury-marred, group of linebackers including Cade Uluave (61 tackles, 2.5 sacks, one interception) and Isaiah Glasker; Glasker is out this week. Faletua Satuala is a well-regarded safety, and defensive end Bodie Schoonover leads the defense with eight tackles for loss.
 A sign of balance: BYU ranks around the middle of the Big 12 in interceptions, forced fumbles and fumble recoveries, but no single player has more than one of any of the three.
 KU’s offense came out with a clinical showing in the win over WVU, but Kotelnicki challenged his players this week, telling them, “Our best football’s still ahead of us.”
 “It ain’t linear, you know what I mean?” Kotelnicki said. “But we’re still improving as a football team, which brings me joy as a coach and a teacher, although it wears me out a lot, what it takes sometimes. But it takes what it takes, and I believe that our best football is still ahead of us.”
 NO. 10 BYU COUGARS (8-2, 5-2 BIG 12) VS. KANSAS JAYHAWKS (4-6, 2-5 BIG 12) 
 • David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium, Lawrence, 11 a.m.
 • Broadcast: ABC
 • Radio: Jayhawk Radio Network (in Lawrence, KLWN AM 1320 / K269GB FM 101.7 / KKSW FM 105.9)
 • Betting line: BYU -5.5; over/under 47.5
 • Series history: KU leads 3-0
 KEEP AN EYE OUT 
 1. The worm: KU has not necessarily dealt well with early kickoffs in recent years. The Jayhawks haven’t won a game with an 11 a.m. Central time start since Oct. 28, 2023, and the stretch of nine losses in that time slot (or eight if you exclude the Union Jack Classic, a night game local time) includes some pretty pivotal matchups that included brutal performances by the Jayhawks — 2024 Baylor and 2025 Kansas State and Iowa State come to mind. KU will need to reverse this trend while also grappling with the heightened emotions of its senior day, albeit with a smaller class of seniors than usual.
 2. Well rested: The Jayhawks should at least be fresh for Saturday on defense because they rotated so extensively against West Virginia. Other than safety Corey Gordon, who played 73 snaps, according to Pro Football Focus, with a career-high 11 tackles, no one had to play more than 49 for KU. Not only was it impressive that the Jayhawks maintained such a high level of productivity on that side of the ball against a dynamic offense with little-used reserves playing unusually often, it also helped lighten the workload for some key players. That’s particularly important as KU hasn’t enjoyed a bye week since early October. The likes of Leroy Harris III, Blake Herold and Trey Lathan played fewer snaps than in any other conference contest, and perhaps they’ll have some extra juice for BYU.
 3. Slipping away: Somewhat surprisingly given its overall defensive numbers, BYU is not a great tackling team. PFF ranks the Cougars 128th of 138 teams in tackling overall, and Uluave, as many tackles as he has made, leads the nation in missed tackles with 26. The Jayhawks have tried to get their playmakers in space with a variety of screen passes, and it hasn’t always worked, but this wouldn’t be the week to deviate from that sort of strategy given that the Cougars can be vulnerable to letting ball carriers by.
 SPOTLIGHT ON… 
 Isaiah Marshall: BYU stops the run extremely well and the Jayhawks could be down as many as five running backs this week. It is as important this week as in any game this year that Marshall demonstrate what he is capable of as a passer. He’s done it in fits and spurts, but too often doesn’t find a rhythm until KU has already fallen behind. The first-year starter still deals with occasional rookie mistakes — an underthrown interception against WVU, for example — but they have at least become less frequent as the year has progressed, and his touch in general is getting better. As Kotelnicki said this week, “When you think about high-level elite quarterbacks, you think about Hall of Fame NFL quarterbacks, they just keep playing and they keep getting better and they keep getting better and keep getting better. And so he’s at the, we hope, early part of his football career as a starting quarterback at a high level, and he is continuing to grow.”
 INSIDE THE NUMBERS 
 83.8%: BYU’s win percentage since 2024, which ranks fifth nationally.
 82.1: Left guard Amir Herring’s PFF grade in his return to the starting lineup in place of the injured Connor Stroh, which was the best single-game grade of his career. It put him third among all Jayhawks against the Mountaineers, behind Marshall and Harris.
 0-1: KU’s record in games played on ABC under Leipold; the first was a 40-14 loss at Texas in 2023.
 PREDICTION 
 BYU wins 21-17. KU’s defense has the tools to limit Bachmeier, but on the other side of the ball, BYU will present a challenge the likes of which KU’s offense hasn’t surmounted yet this season.
 Sports reporter David Rodish contributed to this story.
